The tested production manager computes liquidity as uint128 and widens it to uint256 in action encoding; the fake manager narrows that supplied test value back to uint128. The fake public method itself has no general uint128 width guard and would truncate hostile arbitrary direct liq calldata. This is an explicit fixture limitation, not approved production behavior.

_mintOrIncrease() validates deadline in [block.timestamp,block.timestamp+600] before _approve(). There is no explicit deadline<=uint48.max guard. Contemporary conventional Unix timestamps fit48bits (about 8.9 million years). Retain this chain timestamp-range assumption rather than claiming an unconditional explicit width check.

The uint256 timestamp addition is checked, but narrowing earliest to uint64 has no explicit width guard. Conventional Unix block timestamps plus 2 days are far below2^64 seconds (roughly 584 billion years). This is a timestamp-range assumption, not a mathematical proof for arbitrary uint256/EVM chain timestamps; include it in new-chain/configuration review.

swap() rejects amountIn==0 or amountIn>uint128.max before building the committed pending payload. unlockCallback requires the fixed PoolManager and that exact payload hash. Authorized amountIn therefore fits signed int256 before negation.

Core BalanceDelta is two signed int128 values packed into int256. Shifting the high lane and masking/reinterpreting the low 128 bits deliberately extracts those lanes, matching BalanceDeltaLibrary sar/signextend. The unsigned intermediate preserves bit representation, not an unsigned economic amount; sign/amount checks follow decoding.
